“Perfectly charming!” Mrs. Clay exclaimed, though she dared not direct a glance towards Anne. “Just like a father and son! My dear Miss Elliot, surely I may say father and son?”

“Oh, I impose no restraint on anybody's language. If you choose to entertain such notions! But, upon my honour, I hardly perceive his attentions to be greater than those of other gentlemen.”

“My dear Miss Elliot!” cried Mrs. Clay, throwing up her eyes and hands, and conveniently leaving the remainder of her astonishment unspoken.

“Well, dear Penelope, there is no need to be so concerned on his behalf. I invited him, you know. I dismissed him with smiles. Once I discovered that he really intended spending all to-morrow with his friends at Thornberry Park, I took compassion upon him.”

Anne could admire the friend's excellent performance, displaying such pleasure both in anticipating and in witnessing the arrival of the very person whose presence must interfere with her principal design. Mrs. Clay could not but dislike seeing Mr. Elliot. Nevertheless, she assumed a most accommodating and tranquil expression, appearing fully content to have her liberty curtailed and to bestow upon Sir Walter only half the devotion she would otherwise have offered.

Anne herself found Mr. Elliot's entrance deeply distressing, and his approach and conversation positively painful. Previously she had felt that he could not always be wholly sincere; now every action seemed insincere. His solicitous respect for her father, measured against his earlier language, was detestable. Recalling his cruel treatment of Mrs. Smith, she could scarcely endure his present smiles and gentleness or listen to his counterfeit virtuous sentiments.

She wished to avoid any change of manner sufficiently marked to draw a protest from him. Escaping inquiry or public disturbance mattered greatly to her. Yet she intended to treat him with as much decided coolness as their connection permitted, and quietly to withdraw from the few steps of needless intimacy into which she had gradually been drawn. Consequently, she was more reserved and distant than on the preceding evening.

He hoped to revive her curiosity concerning where and how he had formerly heard her praised, and longed for the gratification of being pressed for particulars. But his spell was broken. He discovered that the warmth and bustle of a public room were required to awaken his modest cousin's vanity; at least he discovered that he could not awaken it now by any approach he dared attempt amid the overly pressing demands of the others.

My heart pounding with a fear I could not explain, I dismissed the servant, locked my door, and sat down to read my father's letter. It contained these words.

“My dear Child,

“I have betrayed your trust. I have tried to corrupt your mind and exposed your innocent heart to the looks and language of a forbidden, monstrous passion. I must atone for these crimes and try to make my punishment, in some measure, equal to my guilt. I have no doubt you are prepared for what I must tell you: we must separate, forever.

“I am taking away your parent and your only friend. I am sending you into the world without protection. Your hopes are ruined, the peace and safety of your innocent mind destroyed. Memory will bring you terrible images of guilt and the pain of innocent love betrayed. Yet I, who bring all this misery upon you; I, who cast you out and have mercilessly stamped distrust and anguish upon my own child's heart and face; I, who with devilish recklessness have tried to steal her beauty and replace it with the hideous deformity of sin—I beg you, from the overwhelming anguish of my heart, to forgive me.

“I do not ask for pity. You must despise me, and you do. But forgive me, Mathilda, and do not let your thoughts pursue me into exile with unrelenting anger. I must never see you again or hear your voice. Yet the gentle whisper of your forgiveness will reach me and soothe the burning of my troubled mind and heart. I am certain I would feel it even in the grave. I dare to support this request by explaining how miserably I was drawn into this net of burning anguish, and how I struggled to escape. Indeed, if your soul were less pure and radiant, I would not try to excuse myself to you. I would fear that, by teaching you to abhor me less, I might weaken your hatred of wrongdoing. But in speaking to you, I feel as though I appeal to an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your forgiveness. I must try to win it or surrender to despair. I beg you, therefore, to hear me. If good people can regard guilt as lessened at all by acute suffering and remorse that tears through the mind like madness, perhaps you may believe, though I dare not, that I have some claim to your compassion.

“Please remember our first happy life beside Loch Lomond. I had returned from sixteen weary years of wandering. Throughout those years, despite the many dangers and misfortunes I encountered, my emotional life had remained completely empty.

“April 19th. At about nine this morning, to my immense delight, the condenser's pump at last showed unmistakable evidence of a change in the atmosphere. The moon's surface was by then fearfully close, and my apprehension had reached its height. By ten I had grounds for believing the air considerably denser. At eleven the apparatus demanded scarcely any labour; and at noon, not without hesitation, I ventured to loosen the tourniquet. Experiencing no discomfort from this, I eventually flung open the gum-elastic chamber and removed its rigging from around the car. As could readily have been foreseen, so rash and hazardous an experiment brought immediate spasms and a violent headache. These, however, and the other impediments to breathing did not appear serious enough to threaten my life. I resolved to bear them as well as possible, since each moment of my advance towards the denser layers near the moon would leave them farther behind. Yet my approach remained exceedingly impetuous. It soon became distressingly clear that, though I had probably judged correctly in expecting an atmosphere whose density corresponded to the satellite's mass, I had erred in supposing that even at the surface it would suffice to support the considerable weight within my balloon's car. Nevertheless, it ought to have done so, and as fully as at the earth's surface, supposing the actual gravity of objects at each planet proportional to the condensation of the atmosphere. My headlong descent testified plainly enough that it did not; the reason could only be sought in those possible geological disturbances to which I have previously referred. In any case, I was now very near the planet and falling with terrifying violence. Accordingly, without a moment's delay, I cast out my ballast first, then the water-kegs, then the condenser and gum-elastic chamber, and at last every object remaining in the car. All proved useless. I continued to drop with dreadful speed and was already within half a mile of the surface. As a final expedient, I threw away my hat, coat, and boots and cut the car itself from the balloon, its weight being by no means trifling. Hanging by both hands from the netting, I had scarcely time to notice that the entire countryside within sight was thickly dotted with tiny dwellings before I plunged head foremost into the centre of a fantastical city. I landed amid a vast gathering of ugly little people. None uttered a word or troubled to offer the slightest assistance; they merely stood like so many idiots, grinning absurdly and looking sideways at me and my balloon, their hands planted upon their hips.
